title: Using Input with Strings, Maps, Sets, and Structs
summary: Parse input lines with string streams and load the data into maps, sets, and vectors of structs.
intro: Reading values is only half the job. Real programs split lines into fields, count what they read, answer questions about it, and keep records together. This lesson connects `std::cin` to the containers you already know.

steps.title: Parsing lines with std::istringstream

example.title: Score lines
example.prompt: Read lines of comma-separated scores and print each name with its total and count.
example.output:
alice 252 (3 scores)
bob 150 (2 scores)
cara 100 (1 score)
example.explanation: The outer loop reads one whole line per pass until the input ends. A fresh `std::istringstream` is built from each line, so every line starts reading from its beginning. The first `getline` with `','` takes the name. The inner loop takes each remaining part, converts it with `std::stoi`, and adds it to `total`. When the line runs out, the next `getline` fails, the stream turns `false`, and the loop stops. The ternary picks `score` or `scores` for the count.

practice.title: Rainfall lines
practice.prompt:
Read rainfall lines until the input ends and print a summary for each day.

1. Read each line with `std::getline(std::cin, line)`. A line looks like `mon,3,4,5`: a day, then any number of readings, possibly none.
2. Wrap the line in a `std::istringstream` and read the day up to the first comma.
3. Read every remaining part with `std::getline(iss, part, ',')`, convert it with `std::stoi`, and add it to a total while counting the parts.
4. Print the day, the total, and the count as `mon 12 (3 readings)`. Write `reading` when the count is exactly 1.

Input:

```text
mon,3,4,5
tue,0,2
wed,7
```

Expected output:

```text
mon 12 (3 readings)
tue 2 (2 readings)
wed 7 (1 reading)
```

tests.output:
mon 12 (3 readings)
tue 2 (2 readings)
wed 7 (1 reading)

hints: Build `std::istringstream iss(line);` inside the line loop so each line starts fresh.
Call `std::getline(iss, day, ',')` once for the day, then loop `while (std::getline(iss, part, ','))` for the readings.
A ternary on `count == 1` can choose between the singular and plural word.

steps.title: Counting input with a map

example.title: Word counts
example.prompt: Count every word in the input, print the counts alphabetically, and name the most frequent word.
example.explanation: `std::cin >> word` skips spaces and newlines, so the two input lines read as five words. `++counts[word]` creates each new word with 0 and then adds 1. The range-for visits blue, green, red in sorted order. blue reaches 2 first and becomes the best. red also has 2, but 2 is not strictly greater than 2, so blue keeps the lead.

practice.title: Vote counter
practice.prompt:
Count votes from the input and announce the winner.

1. Read names with `while (std::cin >> name)` until the input ends and count them with `++votes[name]`.
2. Loop over the map and print each candidate and their votes as `ana 3`, one per line.
3. In the same loop, keep the candidate with the most votes, replacing them only on a strictly greater count.
4. Print `winner: NAME` with the winner's name. On a tie the alphabetically first name wins.

Input:

```text
ana ben ana
cy ben ana
```

Expected output:

```text
ana 3
ben 2
cy 1
winner: ana
```

tests.stdin:
ana ben ana
cy ben ana

hints: `++votes[name]` inside the read loop does all the counting.
Start `winnerVotes` at 0 and replace the winner only when `count > winnerVotes`.

steps.title: Sets for membership queries

example.title: Number lookup
example.prompt: Read n numbers into a set, answer q membership queries, then print the distinct numbers in order.
example.explanation: The first loop reads six numbers, but the set keeps only 1, 3, 5, and 9 because repeated inserts do nothing. The second section starts with `q`, the number of queries. Each query is answered with `count`. The final loop prints the set in ascending order, with `first` making sure a space goes only between values.

practice.title: Login check
practice.prompt:
Check login attempts against a list of registered users.

1. Read `n`, then `n` usernames into a `std::set<std::string>` called `registered`.
2. Read `q`, then `q` login attempts one at a time.
3. For each attempt, print `welcome NAME` when `registered` contains it and `unknown NAME` when it does not.
4. Insert every successful name into a second set, `loggedIn`, so repeat logins count once.
5. Finally print `logged in: COUNT`, where COUNT is the size of `loggedIn`.

Input:

```text
4
ana ben cy ben
5
ben dan ana ben eve
```

Expected output:

```text
welcome ben
unknown dan
welcome ana
welcome ben
unknown eve
logged in: 2
```

tests.stdin:
4
ana ben cy ben
5
ben dan ana ben eve
tests.output:
welcome ben
unknown dan
welcome ana
welcome ben
unknown eve
logged in: 2

unknown bob
unknown tom
logged in: 0

welcome sam
welcome sam
welcome sam
logged in: 1

hints: Use one counted loop for the usernames and a second counted loop for the attempts.
`registered.count(attempt) == 1` is true when the user exists.
A set ignores repeated inserts, so `loggedIn.size()` counts each user once.

steps.title: Records into a vector of structs

example.title: Player ranking
example.prompt: Read player records, rank them by score with ties broken by name, and print the ranking.
example.explanation: Each pass reads three fields straight into a `Player` and pushes a copy into the vector. Age is read because it is part of each line, even though the ranking does not print it. The comparator puts higher scores first. ava and mia both have 88, so the second rule puts ava first. The index loop prints the rank as `i + 1` and lets `print()` write the rest.

practice.title: Movie list
practice.prompt:
Read movies into a vector of structs and list them in release order.

1. Read `n`, then `n` lines of `title year rating` straight into the fields of a `Movie`, and `push_back` each one.
2. Sort with a comparator lambda: earlier year first, and alphabetical title when the years match.
3. Finish the `const` member function `print()` so it prints `year title rating` with the rating to 1 decimal.
4. Call `print()` on every movie in sorted order.

Input:

```text
4
up 2009 8.3
alien 1979 8.5
heat 1995 8.3
casino 1995 8.2
```

Expected output:

```text
1979 alien 8.5
1995 casino 8.2
1995 heat 8.3
2009 up 8.3
```
hints: Copy the shape of the Player loop: declare a `Movie`, read its three fields with one chained `>>`, then `push_back` it.
In the comparator, compare years first and only compare titles when the years are equal.
`std::fixed << std::setprecision(1)` is already set at the top of `main`, so `print()` can stream `rating` directly.

recap:
- `std::istringstream iss(line)` from `<sstream>` turns a line into a stream.
- `std::getline(iss, part, ',')` splits on a delimiter: read the label first, then loop over the rest and convert with `std::stoi`.
- `iss >> token` reads space-separated words, like `std::cin`.
- `++counts[key]` counts while reading, and a `std::map` prints the counts in sorted key order.
- Replace the best only on a strictly greater count so ties go to the alphabetically first key.
- A `std::set` removes duplicates and sorts, and `count` answers membership queries in O(log n).
- Read two sections with two counted loops: `n` items, then `q` queries.
- Read fields straight into struct members, store the structs in a `std::vector`, and sort with a lambda that breaks ties.
- Print records with a `const` member function.
